--- title: "🚧Latent Variable Models" description: "Models that relate a set of observable variables to a set of unobserved (latent) variables." categories: [Factor Analysis] image: "Figures/25.png" order: 22 reading-time: true --- ## General Principles In some scenarios, the observed data does not directly reflect the underlying structure or factors influencing the outcome. Instead, _latent variables_—variables that are not directly observed but are inferred from the data—can help model this hidden structure. These latent variables capture unobserved factors that affect the relationship between predictors (_X_) and the outcome (_Y_). We model the relationship between the predictor variables (_X_) and the outcome variable (_Y_) with a latent variable (_Z_) as follows: $$ Y = f(X, Z) + \epsilon $$ Where: - _Y_ is the observed outcome variable. - _X_ is the observed predictor variable(s). - _Z_ is the latent (unobserved) variable, which we aim to infer. - _f(X, Z)_ is the function that relates _X_ and _Z_ to _Y_. - _\epsilon_ is the error term, typically assumed to be normally distributed with mean 0 and variance _\sigma^2_. The latent variable _Z_ can represent various phenomena, such as group-level effects, time-varying trends, or individual-level factors, that are not captured by the observed predictors alone. ## Considerations In Bayesian regression with latent variables, we consider the uncertainty in both the observed and latent variables. We declare prior distributions for the latent variables, in addition to the usual priors for regression coefficients and intercepts. These latent variables are often modeled using Gaussian distributions (_Normal_ priors) or more flexible distributions such as _Multivariate Normal_ for correlations among the latent variables. The goal is to infer the posterior distribution over both the parameters and the latent variables, given the observed data. ## Example Below is an example code snippet demonstrating Bayesian regression with latent variables using TensorFlow Probability: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#abf82f17 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax.numpy as jnp # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = bf(platform='cpu') # Data Simulation ------------------------------------------------ NY = 4 # Number of dependent variables or outcomes (e.g., dimensions for latent variables) NV = 8 # Number of observations or individual-level data points (e.g., subjects) N = 100 K = 5 a = 0.5 # Generate the means and offsets for the data # means: Generate random normal means for each of the NY outcomes # offsets: Generate random normal offsets for each of the NV observations means = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(NY,), sample=True, seed=10) offsets = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(NV, 1), sample=True, seed=20) # observation noise (sd 0.5) noise = m.dist.normal(0, 0.5, shape=(NV, NY), sample=True, seed=30) Y2 = offsets + means + noise # Simulate individual-level random effects (e.g., random slopes or intercepts) # b_individual: A matrix of size (N, K) where N is the number of individuals and K is the number of covariates b_individual = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(N, K), sample=True, seed=0) # mu: Add an additional effect 'a' to the individual-level random effects 'b_individual' # 'a' could represent a population-level effect or a baseline mu = b_individual + a # Convert Y2 to a JAX array for further computation in a JAX-based framework Y2 = jnp.array(Y2) # Set data ------------------------------------------------ dat = dict( NY = NY, NV = NV, Y2 = Y2 ) m.data_on_model = dat # Define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(NY, NV, Y2): means = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(NY,), name='means') offset = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(NV, 1), name='offset') sigma = m.dist.exponential(1, shape=(NY,), name='sigma') tmp = jnp.tile(means, (NV, 1)).reshape(NV, NY) mu_l = tmp + offset m.dist.normal(mu_l, jnp.tile(sigma, [NV, 1]), obs=Y2) # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, progress_bar=False) # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` An NVIDIA GPU may be present on this machine, but a CUDA-enabled jaxlib is not installed. ``` ::: ::: ## R ```r library(BayesForge) jnp <- reticulate::import("jax.numpy") # Setup device ------------------------------------------------ m <- importBF(platform = "cpu") # Data Simulation ------------------------------------------------ NY <- 4L # Number of dependent variables or outcomes (e.g., dimensions for latent variables) NV <- 8L # Number of observations or individual-level data points (e.g., subjects) N <- 100L K <- 5L a <- 0.5 means <- m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(NY), sample = TRUE, seed = 10L) offsets <- m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(NV, 1L), sample = TRUE, seed = 20L) noise <- m$dist$normal(0, 0.5, shape = reticulate::tuple(NV, NY), sample = TRUE, seed = 30L) Y2 <- offsets + means + noise b_individual <- m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(N, K), sample = TRUE, seed = 0L) mu <- b_individual + a Y2 <- jnp$array(Y2) # Set data ------------------------------------------------ m$data_on_model <- list(NY = NY, NV = NV, Y2 = Y2) # Define model ------------------------------------------------ model <- function(NY, NV, Y2) { means <- m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(NY), name = "means") offset <- m$dist$normal(0, 1, shape = reticulate::tuple(NV, 1L), name = "offset") sigma <- m$dist$exponential(1, shape = reticulate::tuple(NY), name = "sigma") tmp <- jnp$reshape(jnp$tile(means, reticulate::tuple(NV, 1L)), reticulate::tuple(NV, NY)) mu_l <- tmp + offset m$dist$normal(mu_l, jnp$tile(sigma, list(NV, 1L)), obs = Y2, name = "y") } # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m$fit(model, progress_bar = FALSE) # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m$summary() ``` ## Julia ```julia using PyBayesForge using PythonCall # Setup device ------------------------------------------------ m = importBF(platform="cpu") # Data Simulation ------------------------------------------------ NY = 4 # Number of dependent variables or outcomes (e.g., dimensions for latent variables) NV = 8 # Number of observations or individual-level data points (e.g., subjects) N = 100 K = 5 a = 0.5 means = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(NY,), sample=true, seed=10) offsets = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(NV, 1), sample=true, seed=20) noise = m.dist.normal(0, 0.5, shape=(NV, NY), sample=true, seed=30) Y2 = offsets + means + noise b_individual = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(N, K), sample=true, seed=0) mu = b_individual + a Y2 = jnp.array(Y2) # Set data ------------------------------------------------ m.data_on_model = pydict(NY = NY, NV = NV, Y2 = Y2) # Define model ------------------------------------------------ @BF function model(NY, NV, Y2) means = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(NY,), name="means") offset = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(NV, 1), name="offset") sigma = m.dist.exponential(1, shape=(NY,), name="sigma") tmp = jnp.reshape(jnp.tile(means, (NV, 1)), (NV, NY)) mu_l = tmp + offset m.dist.normal(mu_l, jnp.tile(sigma, (NV, 1)), obs=Y2, name="y") end # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, progress_bar=false) # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() ``` ::: ##
